properties.evidence: n = 40 is an integer >= 0 at which n^2 + n + 41 = 1681 = 41·41 is not prime, so 'prime for every n >= 0' is false.
EVIDENCE ONLY: the first 40 cases (n = 0..39) agree with the conjecture. Agreement in finitely many cases does not prove a statement about every n, and n = 40 shows it is false.
Every n = 41m with m >= 1 gives a value divisible by 41 and larger than 41, so the conjecture fails at infinitely many n (n = 41 is the first).

properties.name: Axiom: mathematical induction
properties.statement: If a statement S(n) holds for n = 1, and for every n >= 1 S(n) implies S(n+1), then S(n) holds for every integer n >= 1.

properties.name: Axiom: arithmetic and order of the integers
properties.statement: The integers with + and · form a commutative ring with 1 (associative, commutative, distributive, including over subtraction). They are totally ordered, compatibly with + and ·: the sum and product of positive integers are positive, 1 is the least positive integer, and if x <= y and 0 < z then x·z <= y·z. The product of an empty list of integers is 1.

properties.name: Axiom: pigeonhole principle
properties.statement: A complete list x1, ..., xk of k elements (k >= 0) cannot contain k + 1 pairwise different values.

properties.name: Axiom: well-ordering of the positive integers
properties.statement: Every nonempty set of positive integers has a least element.

properties.name: Definition: divides
properties.statement: For integers a and b, a divides b (written a | b) when b = a·c for some integer c. A divisor of b is an integer that divides b.

properties.name: Definition: Fermat number
properties.statement: For each integer n >= 0, the n-th Fermat number is F_n = 2^(2^n) + 1.

properties.name: Definition: finite and infinite set
properties.statement: A set is finite when its elements can be listed completely as x1, ..., xk for some integer k >= 0 (k = 0 is the empty set). A set is infinite when it is not finite. 'There are infinitely many primes' means: the set of primes is infinite.

properties.name: Definition: prime
properties.statement: A prime is an integer p > 1 whose only positive divisors are 1 and p.

properties.decision: Every statement to be shown (the theorem, Lemmas 1-6, Claims E1-E5 and C) is a Requirement named 'Theorem: ...', 'Lemma n: ...' or 'Claim ...: ...', with no `kind` (none of functional/nonfunctional/quality/business fits a mathematical statement). Every definition and axiom is a Constraint named 'Definition: ...' or 'Axiom: ...'. Every proof step is an Inference (add_inference) with rule `all`, a rule_name naming the logical rule, and a warrant; steps are left unconfirmed for the owner.
properties.name: How this proof is recorded (proposed for the owner to accept)
properties.no_relation_note: The encoding decision governs every statement, definition and axiom of the proof through GOVERNED_BY edges; it relates to no other idea in this design.
properties.rationale: Follows the mathematics vocabulary reflow2 itself serves (theorem/lemma = Requirement, definition/axiom = Constraint, proof step = Inference). Recorded once so each later statement cites this instead of re-deciding.

properties.decision: QUESTION FOR ANTHONY: The heart of the proof (Lemma 6, Euclid) is direct: any finite list of primes misses a prime. The design then closes by contradiction (Claim C, then the theorem), because the textbook form is a reductio and reflow2 cannot hold a discharged assumption, so the supposition 'finitely many primes' lives only inside Claim C's statement and the warrants. Keep this two-step contradiction ending, or conclude the theorem directly from Lemma 6 and the definition of finite in one step?
properties.name: Open question for the owner: keep the final step as proof by contradiction?
properties.no_relation_note: This is an open question for the owner about inf:finitely-many-is-absurd, inf:theorem-by-contradiction and req:claim-finitely-many-is-absurd. None of the offered relations means 'is a question about', so none is drawn.
properties.rationale: Both are valid; the choice is about which reads better to a checker and how faithfully the design shows the reductio.

properties.decision: QUESTION FOR ANTHONY: The proof takes as axioms (unproved) the ring and order facts of the integers (con:axiom-integer-arithmetic) and the well-ordering of the positive integers (con:axiom-well-ordering). Is that an acceptable floor, or should these be derived from the Peano axioms (or another base) so that fewer statements are taken on trust?
properties.name: Open question for the owner: which foundations are taken as given
properties.no_relation_note: This is an open question for the owner about con:axiom-integer-arithmetic and con:axiom-well-ordering. None of the offered relations means 'is a question about', so none is drawn.
properties.rationale: reasoning_report lists these as what the proof rests on and as premises citing no source; the owner decides whether they stay the floor.

properties.decision: QUESTION FOR ANTHONY: The design reads 'there are infinitely many primes' as 'the set of primes is not finite' (con:def-finite-set). An equivalent and common reading is 'for every integer n there is a prime greater than n'. Is the not-finite reading the one you want shown, or should the second reading be added as a corollary?
properties.name: Open question for the owner: what 'infinitely many' means here
properties.no_relation_note: This is an open question for the owner about con:def-finite-set and req:theorem-infinitely-many-primes. None of the offered relations (CONTRADICTS, EVOLVES_INTO, DEPENDS_ON, CAUSES, TRIGGERS, BLOCKS, DUPLICATES, ANTICIPATES, OBSOLETES, RISKS, MITIGATES, MASKS, VIOLATES) means 'is a question about', so none is drawn.
properties.rationale: The theorem's wording is all the designer was given; the reading chosen fixes what the final step must conclude.

properties.name: Proof of Lemma 2
properties.warrant: d | a gives a = d·x and d | b gives b = d·y for integers x, y. Then b - a = d·y - d·x = d·(y - x) by distributivity over subtraction, and y - x is an integer, so d | (b - a).

properties.name: Proof of Lemma 1
properties.warrant: a | b gives b = a·x and b | c gives c = b·y for integers x, y. Then c = (a·x)·y = a·(x·y) by associativity, and x·y is an integer, so a | c by the definition of divides.

properties.name: Proof of Lemma 3
properties.rule_name: direct proof (unfold the definition, then order facts)
properties.warrant: d | n gives n = d·c for an integer c. Since d > 0 and n > 0, c > 0 (if c <= 0 then d·c <= 0). As 1 is the least positive integer, c >= 1, and multiplying by d > 0 gives n = d·c >= d·1 = d.

properties.name: Proof of Lemma 6 (Euclid)
properties.warrant: Claims E1 to E5 were shown for an arbitrary finite list of primes, using nothing about the list except that its members are prime (k = 0 included: then N = 2 and q = 2). Claim E4 gives a prime q and Claim E5 says it is not on the list. Since the list was arbitrary, every finite list of primes misses some prime.

properties.name: Proof of Claim E1
properties.warrant: Each listed pi is prime, so pi > 1 > 0 by definition. A product of positive integers is positive, and the empty product is 1, so P > 0, hence P >= 1 (1 is the least positive integer). Therefore N = P + 1 >= 2.

properties.name: Proof of Claim X (the counterexample)
properties.warrant: The kept computation gives 40^2 + 40 + 41 = 1681 = 41·41, so 41 | 1681 by the definition of divides, with 1 < 41 < 1681. So 1681 has a positive divisor other than 1 and itself and is not prime.

properties.name: Proof of Lemma M
properties.warrant: With n = 41m: n^2 + n + 41 = 41^2·m^2 + 41·m + 41 = 41·(41m^2 + m + 1) by distributivity, so 41 divides it. For m >= 1, 41m^2 + m + 1 > 1, so the value is greater than 41; and 41 > 1. So 41 is a positive divisor other than 1 and the value itself, and the value is not prime.

properties.name: Proof of Claim P (exhaustive check)
properties.warrant: The kept computation shows each value v = n^2 + n + 41 (n = 0..39) satisfies 41 <= v <= 1601 < 41·41 and has no divisor d with 2 <= d <= 40. If such v were not prime, Lemma S would give a divisor d >= 2 with d·d <= v < 41·41, so d <= 40, a contradiction. And v > 1. So each v is prime. This proves the 40 cases only.

properties.name: Proof of Claim F3
properties.warrant: Let m < n and d > 0 divide both F_m and F_n. F_m is one factor of F_0·...·F_(n-1), which equals F_n - 2 by Lemma F2, so F_m | (F_n - 2) by the definition. From d | F_m, Lemma 1 gives d | (F_n - 2). With d | F_n, Lemma 2 gives d | (F_n - (F_n - 2)) = 2.

properties.name: Proof of Lemma F4
properties.warrant: Take m different from n, say m < n. If a prime p divided both, Claim F3 gives p | 2, so p <= 2 (Lemma 3), and p > 1 (prime), so p = 2. But 2 does not divide F_m (Claim F1). So no prime divides both.

properties.name: Proof of Claim F5
properties.rule_name: universal instantiation, then substitution of equals
properties.warrant: Each F_n >= 3 >= 2 (Claim F1), so Lemma 5 gives it a prime divisor q_n. If q_m = q_n for m different from n, that prime would divide both F_m and F_n, which Lemma F4 rules out. So q_0, ..., q_k are pairwise different primes.

properties.name: Proof of Claim F1
properties.rule_name: direct proof, then modus tollens for oddness
properties.warrant: 2^n >= 1, so x = 2^(2^n) = 2·2^(2^n - 1) is a multiple of 2 and x >= 2; hence F_n = x + 1 >= 3. If 2 divided F_n, then as 2 | x, Lemma 2 gives 2 | (F_n - x) = 1, and Lemma 3 gives 2 <= 1, which is false. So 2 does not divide F_n.

properties.name: Proof of Claim F2a
properties.warrant: By the definition, F_0 = 2^1 + 1 and F_1 = 2^2 + 1; the kept computation fermat-product-base-case.calc.json evaluates them exactly as 3 and 5, and F_1 - 2 = 3 = F_0. The product of the single earlier Fermat number F_0 is F_0 itself.

properties.name: Proof of Lemma F2
properties.warrant: S(n): F_0·...·F_(n-1) = F_n - 2. Claim F2a is S(1), Claim F2b is 'S(n) implies S(n+1)' for every n >= 1, so by induction S(n) holds for every n >= 1.

properties.name: Proof of Claim F2b
properties.warrant: Write x = 2^(2^n), so F_n = x + 1 and F_n - 2 = x - 1. Assuming F_0·...·F_(n-1) = F_n - 2, multiply both sides by F_n: F_0·...·F_n = (x - 1)(x + 1) = x^2 - 1. And x^2 = 2^(2·2^n) = 2^(2^(n+1)), so x^2 - 1 = F_(n+1) - 2.

properties.name: Proof of Claim C
properties.rule_name: universal instantiation (the list := all the primes)
properties.warrant: Suppose, for the sake of argument, the set of primes is finite. By the definition of finite it can be listed completely as p1, ..., pk. Lemma 6 applied to this list gives a prime not on it, while the list contains every prime. These two cannot both hold: the supposition leads to a contradiction.

properties.name: Proof of Lemma 4
properties.warrant: D(n) = {d : d > 1 and d | n} is a set of positive integers. It is nonempty: n = n·1 so n | n, and n > 1 because n >= 2, so n is in D(n). By well-ordering D(n) has a least element m(n).

properties.name: Proof of Lemma 5
properties.warrant: Let m = m(n) (Lemma 4), so m > 1 and m | n. Let a be any positive divisor of m with a > 1. From a | m and m | n, Lemma 1 gives a | n, so a is in D(n) and, m being least, a >= m. Lemma 3 gives a <= m. So a = m. Hence the only positive divisors of m are 1 and m, and m > 1, so m is prime by definition; and m divides n.

properties.name: Proof of Claim E2
properties.warrant: By commutativity and associativity, P = pi·c where c is the product of the other listed primes (c = 1 if there are none), an integer. So pi | P by the definition of divides.

properties.name: Proof of Claim E3
properties.warrant: Fix a listed prime pi. If pi | N, then since pi | P (Claim E2), Lemma 2 gives pi | (N - P) = 1. pi and 1 are positive, so Lemma 3 gives pi <= 1. But pi > 1 because pi is prime. So the implication 'pi | N implies pi <= 1' has a false consequent, and pi does not divide N.

properties.name: Proof of Claim E4
properties.rule_name: universal instantiation (n := N), then modus ponens
properties.warrant: Lemma 5 holds for every integer n >= 2; Claim E1 says N >= 2; so N has a prime divisor q.

properties.name: Proof of Claim E5
properties.warrant: q divides N (Claim E4). If q were equal to some listed pi, then pi would divide N, which Claim E3 rules out. So q differs from every listed prime.

properties.name: Proof of Lemma S
properties.rule_name: direct proof (case on the smaller factor)
properties.warrant: v >= 2 not prime means v has a positive divisor a with a different from 1 and v, so 1 < a < v and v = a·b with b an integer; b > 1 since a < v. Let d be the smaller of a and b. Then d >= 2, d | v, and d·d <= a·b = v.

properties.name: Proof of the theorem
properties.warrant: Claim C shows that supposing the set of primes finite leads to a contradiction, so that supposition is false: the set of primes is not finite. By the definition, a set that is not finite is infinite. So there are infinitely many primes. (The supposition itself is never a premise here; only the shown statement Claim C is.)

properties.name: Second proof of the theorem (Goldbach, via Fermat numbers)
properties.warrant: Suppose the set of primes were finite, listed completely as p1, ..., pk. Claim F5 with this k gives k + 1 pairwise different primes q_0, ..., q_k, all of which are on the list of k, which the pigeonhole principle forbids. So the set of primes is not finite, that is, infinite. (Independent of the first proof: it uses none of Claims E1-E5, Lemma 6 or Claim C; it shares only the general Lemmas 1, 2, 3, 5 and the definitions and axioms.)

properties.name: infinitely many primes (proof trial)
properties.objective: A proof that there are infinitely many prime numbers, laid out claim by claim and step by step so a person can read and check the argument and the tool can check its form.

properties.name: Claim E1: N = P + 1 is at least 2
properties.statement: Let p1, ..., pk (k >= 0) be any finite list of primes, P = p1·p2·...·pk (P = 1 when k = 0) and N = P + 1. Then N >= 2.

properties.name: Claim X (counterexample): at n = 40 the value is 41 x 41
properties.statement: At n = 40, n^2 + n + 41 = 1681 = 41·41, which is not prime.

properties.name: Claim P (proven, finite): n^2 + n + 41 is prime for n = 0 to 39
properties.statement: For every integer n with 0 <= n <= 39, n^2 + n + 41 is prime. This is a finite statement shown by exhaustive check; as support for the Conjecture it is EVIDENCE only, never a proof of it.

properties.name: Claim F3: a common divisor of two Fermat numbers divides 2
properties.statement: For 0 <= m < n, every positive common divisor of F_m and F_n divides 2.

properties.name: Claim F5: k + 1 Fermat numbers give k + 1 different primes
properties.statement: For every k >= 0, choosing for each n = 0, ..., k a prime divisor q_n of F_n gives k + 1 pairwise different primes q_0, ..., q_k.

properties.name: Claim F1: every Fermat number is odd and at least 3
properties.statement: For every n >= 0, F_n >= 3 and 2 does not divide F_n.

properties.name: Claim F2a: product formula, base case
properties.statement: F_0 = F_1 - 2 (both equal 3): the product formula of Lemma F2 holds for n = 1.

properties.name: Claim F2b: product formula, inductive step
Claim C: assuming finitely many primes leads to a contradiction
properties.statement: If the set of primes were finite, a contradiction would follow: list all primes as p1, ..., pk; Lemma 6 gives a prime not on that list, yet the list holds every prime.

properties.name: Claim E2: each listed prime divides P
properties.statement: For the list p1, ..., pk and P = p1·...·pk of Claim E1: each listed prime pi divides P.

properties.name: Claim E3: no listed prime divides N
properties.statement: For the list p1, ..., pk and N = P + 1 of Claim E1: no listed prime pi divides N.

properties.name: Claim E4: N has a prime divisor q
properties.statement: For N = P + 1 of Claim E1: N has a prime divisor q.

properties.name: Claim E5: q is not on the list
properties.statement: The prime divisor q of N (Claim E4) is none of p1, ..., pk.

properties.name: Conjecture: n^2 + n + 41 is always prime
properties.statement: For every integer n >= 0, n^2 + n + 41 is prime.

properties.name: Lemma 2: a common divisor divides the difference
properties.statement: For integers d, a, b: if d | a and d | b, then d | (b - a).

properties.name: Lemma 1: divisibility is transitive
properties.statement: For integers a, b, c: if a | b and b | c, then a | c.

properties.name: Lemma 3: a positive divisor is at most the number
properties.statement: If d and n are positive integers and d | n, then d <= n.

properties.name: Lemma 6 (Euclid): no finite list holds every prime
properties.statement: For every finite list of primes p1, ..., pk (k >= 0) there is a prime that is not on the list.

properties.name: Lemma M: the value is not prime whenever n is a positive multiple of 41
properties.statement: For every integer m >= 1, at n = 41m the value n^2 + n + 41 equals 41·(41m^2 + m + 1) and is not prime; so the Conjecture fails for infinitely many n.

properties.name: Lemma F4 (Goldbach): distinct Fermat numbers share no prime divisor
properties.statement: For m different from n, no prime divides both F_m and F_n.

properties.name: Lemma F2: product of the earlier Fermat numbers
Lemma 4: least divisor above 1 exists
properties.statement: For every integer n >= 2, the set D(n) of integers greater than 1 that divide n has a least element; call it m(n).

properties.name: Lemma 5: every integer n >= 2 has a prime divisor
properties.statement: For every integer n >= 2, the least divisor m(n) of n greater than 1 is prime; so n has a prime divisor.

properties.name: Lemma S: a non-prime has a divisor at most its square root
properties.statement: If an integer v >= 2 is not prime, it has a divisor d with d >= 2 and d·d <= v.

properties.name: Theorem: there are infinitely many primes
properties.statement: There are infinitely many prime numbers: the set of primes is infinite (in the sense of con:def-finite-set).

properties.description: flo2-calc computes v = n^2 + n + 41 for n = 0..39 and tests, exactly, whether any integer d from 2 to 40 divides v (v/d equal to floor(v/d)).
properties.findings: No d in 2..40 divides any of the 40 values (composite_count = 0); the values run from 41 to 1601, and 1601 < 1681 = 41·41; every value exceeds 40 (exact).
properties.name: Computation: trial division of n^2 + n + 41 for n = 0 to 39

properties.description: flo2-calc computes 40^2 + 40 + 41 exactly and compares it with 41·41, and checks 1 < 41 < the value.

properties.description: flo2-calc evaluates F_0 = 2^(2^0)+1 and F_1 = 2^(2^1)+1 exactly and compares F_0 with F_1 - 2.
